newsitem.title: JAPAN: Dlr dive halts Japan insurers' foreign bond buying.
newsitem.headline: Dlr dive halts Japan insurers' foreign bond buying.

text.p: The dollar's recent plunge against the yen has halted fresh foreign bond purchases by Japanese life insurance firms, who were previously heavy investors in foreign assets, insurers and traders say.
The dollar fell to a five-month low of 111.98 yen on Tuesday, down some 12 percent from its recent peak of 127.47 yen set on May 1. It was trading around 113.60 yen late on Wednesday.
Major Japanese life insurers were estimated to have bought some two trillion yen ($17.5 billion) in foreign bonds and stocks in fiscal 1996/97, which ended on March 31.
They had planned fresh foreign bond investments of a similar magnitude for the current fiscal year, but the dollar's tumble has forced them to think twice about their portfolios.
"We are completely holding back from fresh U.S. bond investment as the dollar has not shown any sign of stabilising," said a fund manager at a major life insurer.
"Until the dollar confirms its medium-term bottom, we have no plan to boost U.S. bond holdings," the manager said.
"Insurers have been generally quiet amid the dollar's recent falls and uncertainty over the direction of U.S. interest rates," a bond manager at a major brokerage firm said.

Currency traders said the dollar's downward spiral is far from being over, although Japanese monetary authorities have recently signalled that the yen has made a sufficient upward correction, at least in the near-term.

As for U.S. currency policy, the insurer manager said: "I do not think the U.S. wants to stabilise the dollar/yen at the current level as Japanese exporters, in general, are still very competitive at the current rate."
On a stock basis, Japan's cash-rich life insurers held around 17.10 trillion yen ($150 billion) in foreign securities at the end of February this year.

Dealers said insurers' inertia in the foreign bond market may be a sign that they are preoccupied by the fact that they are now exposed to massive currency risks on foreign bond holdings that were not hedged against the dollar's fall.
During the past two years of the strong dollar trend, insurers had been able to pile up foreign bond holdings without a currency hedge or selling U.S. dollars in forward contracts.
Currency dealers said insurers are now likely to try to sell dollars to hedge their foreign-denominated assets, if the dollar rises again versus the yen.
Insurers may start hedging and sell dollars when it rebounds to 116 or 117 yen, which could make the dollar's quick recovery to 120 yen difficult, currency dealers said.
"Life insurers have been the slowest to hedge against currency risks," said an options dealer at a U.S. bank.
But insurance company officials said they would not rush to sell dollars as it could only accelerate the dollar's downward spiral and would widen their foreign exchange losses.
"We were caught off guard by the dollar's steep fall in the past two weeks. But we will not rush to sell cash dollars," said a fund manager at another major life insurance firm.

Insurers generally prefer to use a so-called "zero-cost options" strategy in which they simultaneously buy "call" and sell "put" options with different strike prices to offset the payments of premiums on the buy options.
The option dealer at the U.S. bank said current market conditions would allow insurers to engage in a structure of dollar calls with strikes at 110 yen and puts at 118 yen. ($1=114 yen)
